text: We proposed a new training data-independent framework, called Deep Contextual Features Learning (DeepCFL), to perform image synthesis and image restoration based on the semantics of the input image. The contextual features are simply the high dimensional vectors representing the semantics of the given image.

We introduce a novel training data-independent framework designated Deep Contextual Features Learning (DeepCFL), conceived for the purpose of image synthesis and restoration grounded in the semantic content of the input image. The contextual features constitute high-dimensional vector representations that encode the semantic information present within the given image.

DeepCFL is a single image GAN framework that learns the distribution of the context vectors from the input image. We show the performance of contextual learning in various challenging scenarios: outpainting, inpainting, and restoration of randomly removed pixels.

DeepCFL operates as a single-image generative adversarial network framework that models the distributional characteristics of context vectors derived from a solitary input image. The efficacy of the contextual learning paradigm is demonstrated across a range of demanding tasks including image outpainting, inpainting of arbitrary masked regions, and the reconstruction of randomly ablated pixels.

One of the major challenges for the deep feature learning methods is the limited contextual understanding in the absence of feature learning from training samples. Contextual learning is mostly studied for image inpainting and image transformation tasks, where many pairs of source and target images are used to learn the image context.

A predominant limitation of deep feature learning methods in training-data-free settings is the constrained capacity for contextual comprehension. Contextual learning has been principally investigated in the context of image inpainting and transformation tasks, wherein large collections of paired source and target images facilitate the acquisition of image context representations.

The pixel-to-pixel loss framework and the internal patch distribution learning frameworks do not perform image reconstruction by considering the context of the objects. An image could be considered as a collection of high dimensional context vectors. These high dimensional vectors are the image statistics captured at the intermediate layers of the features extractor such as VGG19 network.

Pixel-wise loss frameworks and internal patch distribution methods are fundamentally limited in their capacity to reconstruct images through contextual object understanding. Conceptualizing an image as an assemblage of high-dimensional context vectors—specifically, the feature statistics extracted at intermediate layers of a pretrained network such as VGG19—enables a richer form of semantic image reconstruction.

CAL performs distribution matching in the adversarial framework to synthesize new context vectors for the corrupted image. CVL computes the direct difference between the context vectors extracted from the corrupted image and the restored image. Therefore, in CFL, CAL generates new context vectors and CVL improvises them.

The contextual adversarial loss facilitates distribution matching within the adversarial framework, enabling the synthesis of novel context vectors for corrupted image regions. The context vector loss directly minimizes the discrepancy between context vectors extracted from the corrupted and restored images respectively. Within the combined contextual features loss, the adversarial component generates candidate context vectors while the direct comparison component refines their quality.

The generator maps the source image to the target image. It is a depth-5 encoder-decoder network without skip connections. The encoder-decoder architecture works as the implicit regularizer to stabilize the image feature learning. It exploits the inherent self-similarity present in the source image.

The generator network performs the mapping from source to target image space using a five-level encoder-decoder architecture devoid of skip connections. This design choice is motivated by the implicit regularization properties of the encoder-decoder structure, which contributes to the stability of feature learning by exploiting the intrinsic self-similarity characteristics of natural images.

DeepCFL outperforms the other methods for outpainting. Table 1 shows the quantitative comparison on the standard datasets. It could be observed that DeepCFL leads in terms of SSIM and PSNR metrics for image outpainting of 20% pixels across standard dataset, Set5, and Set14 datasets.

Quantitative evaluation confirms the superiority of DeepCFL over competing methods on the image outpainting task. Across all three benchmark datasets—the standard dataset, Set5, and Set14—DeepCFL achieves leading performance on both SSIM and PSNR metrics for the task of restoring 20% missing peripheral pixels.

The contextual learning of DeepCFL minimizes the features spillover between different objects and fills the arbitrary holes considering the semantics of the image. The estimation of the parameters from a single image is highly sensitive to the hyper-parameters such as learning rate.

DeepCFL's contextual learning mechanism mitigates cross-object feature bleed, enabling the filling of irregular image holes with semantically coherent content. A notable practical limitation is the heightened sensitivity of single-image parameter estimation to hyperparameter choices, particularly the learning rate, necessitating careful tuning for optimal results.

Data science has become increasingly essential for the production of official statistics, as it enables the automated collection, processing, and analysis of large amounts of data. With such data science practices in place, it enables more timely, more insightful and more flexible reporting.

Data science has emerged as an increasingly indispensable component of official statistics production, enabling the automated collection, processing, and analysis of large-scale data. The integration of data science methodologies facilitates more timely, more informative, and more adaptable statistical reporting compared to conventional approaches.

Changes in data sources are inevitable to occur and pose significant risks that are crucial to address in the context of machine learning for official statistics. The quality and integrity of data-science-driven statistics rely on the accuracy and reliability of the data sources and the machine learning techniques that support them.

Data source changes are an unavoidable occurrence that introduces substantial risks requiring careful consideration within the machine learning pipeline supporting official statistics production. The quality and integrity of data-science-driven statistical products are fundamentally contingent upon the accuracy and reliability of both the underlying data sources and the machine learning methodologies applied to them.

As the popular saying goes: with great power comes great responsibility. Having control and power over your data is essential to fulfilling your responsibilities as a statistics agency. However, in the world of data, the opposite is often true: with great amounts of external data comes great powerlessness.

While data abundance presents considerable analytical opportunities, it paradoxically diminishes the degree of control that statistical agencies can exercise over their data pipelines. Whereas traditional survey-based and administrative data sources are wholly under agency control, the exploitation of external data introduces a fundamental powerlessness that must be explicitly acknowledged and managed.

Concept drift is related to changes in the data distribution between train and test time, which can have multiple causes. A particular pervasive issue is the calculation of derived data fields, especially when those calculations are not transparent or proprietary. You should always assume that derived data fields can be the result of a model prediction.

Concept drift denotes the phenomenon of distributional divergence between training and inference data, arising from diverse sources of temporal change. A particularly insidious manifestation concerns derived data fields whose computational origin is opaque or proprietary—such fields may themselves be produced by upstream machine learning models, meaning that unannounced model updates silently alter the data distribution seen by dependent models.

A change in data frequency refers to modifications made to the rate at which data is collected or updated, which can happen deliberately or randomly. Deliberate changes may arise due to shifts in business requirements or technological choices. Random shifts are most often attributed to noisy factors such as network issues, component failures, downtime, or human errors.

Data collection frequency may be subject to both deliberate and inadvertent modification. Intentional frequency changes typically reflect evolving business requirements or technological transitions, whereas unplanned variations commonly result from infrastructure instability including network disruptions, hardware failures, system downtime, or human operational errors. Either form of frequency change can substantially alter the statistical properties of the data on which machine learning models were trained.

Worse than interruptions is downright discontinuation of the data source, which has immediate consequences on the future existence of the statistic. Also, a change of ownership of the data source is not a fictional scenario, and it can trigger any of the risks that are discussed. Building redundancy by diversifying data sources is a useful mitigating strategy.

Complete discontinuation of a data source represents a more severe outcome than mere interruption, immediately imperiling the future viability of statistics that depend upon it. Ownership transfers—for example, acquisition of a data provider by another organization—constitute a realistic risk scenario capable of triggering any of the aforementioned adverse effects. Diversification across multiple data sources provides a valuable hedge against single-source failure.

Monitoring everything that is relevant is another crucial step in mitigating the impact of changing data sources. It involves tracking various aspects of the data sources, the machine learning models, and their outputs to detect and respond to changes promptly. Supervised models can be tested against a reference test set; if the accuracy, precision or recall starts to deviate significantly, it should be flagged.

Comprehensive monitoring of data sources, model behaviour, and statistical outputs constitutes an essential safeguard against the deleterious effects of data source changes. By continuously tracking performance metrics against reference benchmarks, practitioners can promptly detect distributional shifts and model degradation. For supervised models specifically, statistically significant deviations in accuracy, precision, or recall from reference values should trigger investigation.

We propose an approach to Multitask Learning to make deep learning models faster and lighter for applications in which multiple tasks need to be solved simultaneously, which is particularly useful in embedded, real-time systems. Our multitask network is 1.6x faster, lighter and uses less memory than deploying the single-task models in parallel.

We present a Multitask Learning approach that simultaneously reduces inference latency and model size for applications requiring concurrent resolution of multiple tasks—a setting of particular relevance to resource-constrained embedded systems with real-time processing requirements. The proposed multitask network achieves a 1.6-fold speedup over parallel single-task deployment while correspondingly reducing memory consumption and model storage requirements.

Multitask Learning learns to solve tasks in parallel using a shared representation of a common input, improving the generalization capabilities of the models. Multitask networks share a base trunk and a number of task-specific branches emerging from it. Only the task-specific layers are computed separately.

Multitask Learning exploits a shared input representation to simultaneously optimize for multiple tasks, yielding improved generalization through the inductive transfer of complementary task-specific signals. The architectural paradigm consists of a shared backbone network from which multiple task-specific branches diverge, with computational overhead incurred only for the branch-specific components.

The compromises made due to the particularities of MTL and especially the lack of a strong data augmentation caused the final accuracy of our multitask model to lag behind that of the single-task ones trained without these limitations, although they improved in terms of speed and usage of resources, being 1.6x faster, lighter and consuming less memory.

The accuracy gap between the multitask model and unrestricted single-task baselines is primarily attributable to the inherent training constraints of the multitask setting and the limited data augmentation regime. Despite this accuracy trade-off, the multitask model realizes substantial computational benefits, operating at 1.6 times the throughput of naively combined single-task models while simultaneously reducing memory footprint and parameter storage requirements.

For acute ischemic stroke patients with large vessel occlusions, clinicians must decide if the benefit of mechanical thrombectomy outweighs the risks and potential complications following an invasive procedure. Pre-treatment computed tomography and angiography are widely used to characterize occlusions in the brain vasculature.

Clinicians treating acute ischemic stroke patients presenting with large vessel occlusions must weigh the prospective therapeutic benefit of mechanical thrombectomy against the procedural risks associated with this invasive intervention. Computed tomography and CT angiography obtained prior to treatment serve as the primary imaging modalities for characterizing the nature and extent of cerebrovascular occlusions.

A modified treatment in cerebral ischemia score will be used to grade how well blood flow is reestablished throughout and following the mechanical thrombectomy procedure. An estimation of the likelihood of successful recanalization can support treatment decision-making.

The modified treatment in cerebral ischemia score provides a standardized grading system for quantifying the degree of blood flow restoration achieved by the thrombectomy procedure. Reliable pre-procedural estimation of recanalization likelihood would constitute a valuable clinical decision-support instrument, enabling more informed treatment planning.

We designed a spatial cross attention network that utilizes vision transformers to localize to pertinent slices and brain regions. Our top model achieved an average cross-validated ROC-AUC of 77.33 percent. This is a promising result that supports future applications of deep learning on CT and CTA for the identification of eligible acute ischemic stroke patients.

The proposed spatial cross attention network employs vision transformer modules to achieve automatic localization of diagnostically relevant image slices and cerebrovascular regions. The top-performing model configuration attained a cross-validated ROC-AUC of 77.33 percent, representing a promising result that validates the potential of transformer-based deep learning for automated patient selection for thrombectomy.

A spatial attention transformer utilized multi-head attention on each slice to focus on salient regions. Within each neighborhood branch, a cross attention transformer identified important slices. Finally, the branch outputs were subjected to a weighted softmax layer to ultimately generate binary predictions.

Multi-head self-attention within the spatial attention transformer module directs the model's focus toward diagnostically informative regions within each individual imaging slice. Complementing this, the cross attention transformer operating within each neighborhood branch facilitates identification of the most informative slices along the axial dimension. A weighted softmax aggregation layer synthesizes the branch-level representations into a final binary prediction.

The ability to explain decisions made by machine learning models remains one of the most significant hurdles towards widespread adoption of AI in highly sensitive areas such as medicine, cybersecurity or autonomous driving. Great interest exists in understanding which features of the input data prompt model decision making.

The interpretability of machine learning model decisions constitutes one of the most formidable barriers to the pervasive deployment of artificial intelligence in high-stakes domains, including medical diagnosis, cybersecurity, and autonomous vehicular navigation. Substantial research interest is directed toward identifying which input data characteristics drive model predictions.

By identifying conserved weights within groups of minima of the loss landscapes, we can identify the drivers of model decision making. Analogues to this idea exist in the molecular sciences, where coordinate invariants or order parameters are employed to identify critical features of a molecule.

The identification of conserved weights shared across groups of loss landscape minima provides a mechanism for attributing model decisions to specific input features. This methodology draws conceptual inspiration from the molecular sciences, where coordinate invariants and order parameters serve the analogous function of identifying the critical structural characteristics that define distinct molecular configurations.

A disconnectivity graph is a low-dimensional representation of a complex function landscape, which reduces the function to key characteristic stationary points, namely minima and transition states. The vertical axis of a disconnectivity graph represents the energy or loss value, and ordering along the horizontal axis is arbitrary.

A disconnectivity graph provides a compact, low-dimensional representation of a high-dimensional loss landscape by retaining only the topologically significant stationary points—specifically the local minima and index-1 saddle points (transition states). The vertical axis encodes the energy or loss value, while the horizontal organization of branches is topologically defined rather than geometrically meaningful.

Randomly permuting the conserved weights strongly decreases model performance, much more so than permuting any other random set of weights of equivalent cardinality. This result indicates that the conserved weights identified through energy landscape analysis are indeed critical to model performance.

Stochastic permutation of the identified conserved weights produces a markedly more severe degradation in model performance compared to the equivalent perturbation of a randomly selected weight subset of identical cardinality. This differential sensitivity empirically confirms that the conserved weights isolated through energy landscape methodology are genuinely critical determinants of predictive performance.

Due to smaller zero-evidence region, more expressive gradients, and no issue of learning in high incorrect evidence region, the exponential-based evidential models are expected to be more effective compared to ReLU and SoftPlus based evidential models.

The superiority of exponential-activation evidential models over their ReLU and SoftPlus counterparts is attributable to three complementary advantages: a substantially reduced zero-evidence region, more expressive gradient signals across the evidence space, and the absence of learning pathologies in the high incorrect-evidence regime—limitations that both ReLU and SoftPlus exhibit.

Performing a risk analysis before incorporating a new data source is an essential step in mitigating the impact of changes in data sources. The analysis should be comprehensive, considering both technical and non-technical aspects of the data source, and should ideally include potential solutions for the identified risks.

Conducting a thorough risk assessment prior to integrating any new external data source is an indispensable precautionary step. The assessment must be holistic in scope, addressing both technical vulnerabilities and non-technical considerations such as ownership, ethics, and regulatory compliance, and should ideally enumerate potential mitigation strategies for each identified risk.

Building technical robustness is paramount and requires significant engineering efforts. Building an automated, data-driven statistic that is resistant to changing data sources such as errors, outliers, outages, time-dependent variability ensures consistency in the statistical offering.

The construction of technically robust statistical pipelines demands substantial and sustained engineering investment. An automated statistical product designed to withstand data source perturbations—including erroneous records, statistical outliers, service interruptions, and temporal distributional variability—provides a foundation for consistent and reliable official statistics production.

Agreeing on clear legal guidelines is the best mitigation strategy to counter the risk of changing data sources, for example by closing formal data sharing agreements or SLAs with data providers. Such agreements should specify the terms and conditions under which the data can be shared, as well as the legal responsibilities of each party.

Establishing unambiguous legal frameworks constitutes the most robust strategy for managing data source risk. Formal data sharing agreements and service level agreements with data providers should precisely delineate the conditions governing data access and sharing, articulate the legal obligations of all parties, and specify the consequences of non-compliance including remediation procedures.

The use of machine learning for official statistics has the potential to provide more timely, accurate and comprehensive insights into a wide range of societal topics. By leveraging the vast amounts of data that are generated by individuals and entities on a daily basis, statistical agencies can gain a more nuanced understanding of trends and patterns.

The application of machine learning to official statistics production holds considerable promise for delivering more current, precise, and comprehensive societal insights. By harnessing the enormous volumes of data continuously generated by individuals and organizations, statistical agencies can attain a more granular and nuanced characterization of evolving trends and distributional patterns than is achievable through traditional survey methods.

Supervised learning is one of the most common types of machine learning used for official statistics. This method involves training a model on a labeled dataset, where each data point has a known outcome or target variable. The model learns to associate features in the data with the target variable, enabling it to make predictions on new data.

Supervised learning constitutes the predominant machine learning paradigm applied in official statistics contexts. In this framework, a model is trained on labeled data in which each observation is associated with a known target outcome, enabling the model to learn the predictive relationship between input features and the target variable for subsequent application to unlabeled observations.

Changing data sources can also introduce bias or incorrect data, which can impact the neutrality of the statistics produced. Since it is essential that official statistics remain neutral and objective, this will negatively impact the accuracy and validity of these statistics.

Data source changes carry the risk of introducing systematic biases or erroneous data values into the statistical production pipeline, potentially compromising the neutrality that is a fundamental requirement of official statistics. Any such compromise of objectivity necessarily degrades both the accuracy and the inferential validity of the resulting statistical outputs.

In neural networks, the most popular approach to interpretability is to study the outgoing weights and gradients from an individual input node. Larger weights are reasonably assumed to indicate a greater significance of the particular input, and an entire class of interpretability metrics, namely gradient-based methods, are founded on this idea.

The dominant paradigm for neural network interpretability involves examining the magnitude of weights and gradients associated with individual input features. The intuition that larger weight magnitudes correspond to greater feature relevance underpins an entire family of gradient-based attribution methods, which quantify feature importance through various formulations of the input-output derivative.

Well-established methods from computational chemical physics can be employed to enhance our understanding of machine learning systems. We have shown that groups of minima share conserved weights and importantly, that these weights are critical to model performance.

Methodologies originally developed within computational chemical physics offer valuable tools for illuminating the internal behavior of machine learning systems. The central finding of this work is that clusters of loss landscape minima exhibit conserved weight configurations, and that these conserved weights are disproportionately critical to model performance compared to randomly selected weight subsets.

The discrimination between single image GAN frameworks lies in the different approaches to internal feature learning. DeepCFL uses the adversarial framework on VGG features space for image outpainting, in contrast to DCIL which uses the adversarial framework on the image space for denoising-super resolution.

Single-image GAN frameworks are differentiated by the representational domain in which their adversarial learning operates. DeepCFL performs distribution matching within the high-dimensional VGG feature space, enabling semantic understanding for outpainting tasks, whereas DCIL conducts adversarial training directly in the pixel image space, which is suited to the denoising and super-resolution tasks that framework targets.

Evidential deep learning, built upon belief theory and subjective logic, offers a principled and computationally efficient way to turn a deterministic neural network uncertainty-aware. The resultant evidential models can quantify fine-grained uncertainty using the learned evidence.

Grounded in the foundational principles of belief theory and subjective logic, evidential deep learning furnishes a rigorous and computationally economical methodology for endowing deterministic neural architectures with uncertainty-aware capabilities. The resulting evidential models possess the capacity to quantify uncertainty in a fine-grained manner through the utilization of learned evidential representations.

Deep Learning models have found great success in many real-world applications such as speech recognition, machine translation, and computer vision. However, these highly expressive models may easily fit the noise in the training data, which leads to overconfident predictions.

Deep learning architectures have demonstrated remarkable efficacy across a wide spectrum of real-world domains, encompassing speech recognition, machine translation, and computer vision. Nevertheless, owing to their substantial expressive capacity, such models are susceptible to overfitting noise present in training data, consequently yielding predictions characterized by excessive and unwarranted confidence.

The challenge is further compounded when learning from limited labeled data, which is common for applications from specialized domains such as medicine, public safety, and military operations where data collection and annotation is highly costly. Accurate uncertainty quantification is essential for successful application of DL models in these domains.

The difficulty of reliable learning is substantially amplified in data-scarce regimes, a condition routinely encountered in specialized application domains including medicine, public safety, and defense, where acquiring and annotating data entails prohibitive costs. In such high-stakes settings, accurate quantification of predictive uncertainty becomes an indispensable prerequisite for responsible deployment of deep learning systems.

The recently developed evidential models bring together evidential theory and deep neural architectures that turn a deterministic neural network uncertainty-aware. By leveraging the learned evidence, evidential models are capable of quantifying fine-grained uncertainty that helps to identify the sources of unknowns. Furthermore, since only lightweight modifications are introduced to existing DL architectures, additional computational costs remain minimum.

Contemporary evidential models achieve a synthesis of evidential theory and deep neural network architectures, endowing otherwise deterministic systems with the capacity for uncertainty-aware inference. Through exploitation of learned evidence representations, these models enable nuanced discrimination between distinct sources of uncertainty and identification of what remains unknown. Importantly, the requisite architectural modifications are minimal, ensuring that computational overhead remains negligible.

Evidential classification models formulate training as an evidence acquisition process and consider a higher-order Dirichlet prior over the predictive Multinomial distribution. Different from a standard Bayesian formulation which optimizes Type II Maximum Likelihood to learn the Dirichlet hyperparameter, evidential models directly predict the Dirichlet parameters using data features.

The training paradigm of evidential classification models is conceptualized as a process of evidence accumulation, wherein a higher-order Dirichlet prior is imposed over the predictive multinomial distribution. In marked contradistinction to conventional Bayesian formulations—which optimize Type II Maximum Likelihood for Dirichlet hyperparameter estimation—evidential models directly regress the Dirichlet parameters as a function of the input data features.

In evidential models, the softmax layer of the standard neural networks is replaced by a non-negative activation function, such that for input x, the neural network model can output evidence for different classes. Dirichlet prior is evaluated as alpha equals evidence plus one to ensure alpha is greater than or equal to one.

Evidential models substitute the conventional softmax output layer with a non-negative activation function, enabling the network to output evidence quantities for each class. The Dirichlet concentration parameters are subsequently derived by incrementing the raw evidence values by unity, thereby guaranteeing that all Dirichlet parameters satisfy the required positivity constraint.

Evidential models assign input sample to that class for which the output evidence is greatest. Moreover, they quantify the confidence in the prediction through vacuity, which is a measure of lack of confidence in the prediction. With evidential training, accurate evidential deep learning models are expected to output high evidence for the correct class, low evidence for all other classes, and output very high vacuity for unseen or out-of-distribution samples.

Classification in evidential models is performed by assigning each input to the category associated with the maximal predicted evidence. Predictive confidence is characterized through the notion of vacuity—a scalar quantity inversely related to the overall evidence mass—which captures the degree of epistemic uncertainty. Well-trained evidential models are expected to exhibit concentrated evidence on the ground truth class, suppressed evidence elsewhere, and maximally elevated vacuity when confronted with out-of-distribution or previously unseen inputs.

A Zero-evidence sample is a data sample for which the model outputs zero evidence for all classes. A region in the evidence space that contains zero-evidence samples is a zero-evidence region. For a reasonable evidential model, novel data samples not yet seen during training, difficult data samples, and out-of-distribution samples should become zero-evidence samples.

A zero-evidence sample is formally defined as any data instance for which the model's output evidence is null across all class labels. The collection of such samples within the evidence space constitutes the zero-evidence region. Under a well-designed evidential model, this region should encompass novel unseen instances, particularly challenging samples, and out-of-distribution inputs, for which maximal uncertainty is the appropriate response.

Given a training sample x and y, if an evidential neural network outputs zero evidence, then the gradients of the evidential loss evaluated on this training sample over the network parameters reduce to zero. For zero-evidence training samples, for any node k, the gradient of the loss with respect to the output is zero. Since the gradient of the loss with respect to all the nodes is zero, there is no update to the model from such samples.

The gradient of the evidential loss with respect to all network parameters reduces identically to zero whenever a training sample elicits zero evidence from the network. This gradient collapse occurs uniformly across all output nodes, meaning that zero-evidence training samples contribute absolutely no update signal to the model parameters, effectively rendering such samples invisible to the learning procedure.

For a zero-evidence sample with ReLU activation, the logits satisfy the relationship that all logits are less than or equal to zero, which implies the gradient of evidence with respect to logits is zero, and consequently the loss gradient is zero. For SoftPlus activation, the logits approach negative infinity for zero-evidence samples, making the sigmoid term approach zero. For exponential activation, alpha approaches one making the gradient term approach zero.

Under ReLU activation, zero-evidence conditions correspond to all pre-activation logits being non-positive, directly causing the activation derivative to vanish and eliminating the loss gradient. With SoftPlus activation, zero evidence implies that logits diverge towards negative infinity, driving the sigmoid derivative arbitrarily close to zero. In the case of exponential activation, zero evidence corresponds to Dirichlet parameters approaching unity, which similarly causes the gradient term to vanish asymptotically.

Incorrect evidence regularization can not help evidential models learn from zero-evidence samples. The regularization updates the model parameters such that the model is likely to map input samples closer to zero-evidence region in the evidence space. Thus, the regularization does not address the failure of evidential models to learn from zero evidence samples.

Existing incorrect evidence regularization schemes are fundamentally incapable of resolving the zero-evidence learning deficiency. Rather than alleviating the problem, such regularization terms actively incentivize the model to map training samples toward the zero-evidence region by penalizing incorrect evidence. Consequently, they exacerbate rather than mitigate the underlying failure mode and provide no mechanism for the model to extract knowledge from zero-evidence instances.

We propose a novel vacuity-guided correct evidence regularization term. The regularization term determines the relative importance of the correct evidence regularization compared to the evidential loss and incorrect evidence regularization and is treated as constant during model parameter update.

We introduce a novel vacuity-guided regularization mechanism that specifically targets the correct evidence for the ground truth class. The weighting coefficient of this regularization term governs its proportional influence relative to the primary evidential loss and the incorrect evidence penalty, and is treated as a fixed constant throughout the parameter optimization step.

The gradient value equals the magnitude of the vacuity. The vacuity is bounded in the range zero to one, and for a zero-evidence sample, the vacuity is maximum, leading to the greatest gradient value of negative one. The regularization encourages the model to update the parameters such that the correct evidence increases. As the model evidence increases, the vacuity decreases, and the contribution of the regularization is minimized.

The regularization gradient magnitude is directly proportional to the vacuity, a quantity bounded between zero and unity. At zero-evidence conditions, the vacuity achieves its maximum value, producing the strongest possible regularization signal. This arrangement induces the model to increase the evidence allocated to the ground truth class, with the regularization contribution automatically attenuating as evidence accumulates and vacuity correspondingly diminishes.

The overall loss for the Regularized Evidential model combines the evidential loss, the incorrect evidence regularization, and the proposed correct evidence regularization. The evidential model is trained to maximize the correct evidence, minimize the incorrect evidence, and avoid the zero-evidence region during training.

The training objective of the Regularized Evidential Deep model integrates three complementary components: the core evidential loss, the incorrect evidence penalty, and the proposed correct evidence regularization. This composite objective simultaneously encourages the maximization of evidence assigned to the ground truth class, the suppression of evidence for incorrect classes, and the active avoidance of the zero-evidence region throughout the learning process.

The architectural instantiations employed are LeNet for MNIST, ResNet-18 for the CIFAR datasets, and ResNet-12 for the few-shot classification setting.

However, subsequent progress stagnates as the model maps two training instances to the zero-evidence region, from which no further gradient information can be extracted. This learning failure persists even in the elementary four-sample experimental configuration, providing empirical corroboration of the theoretically established learning deficiency.

We visualize the zero-evidence data samples for the toy dataset setting. The evidential model continues to output zero evidence for two of the training examples and fails to learn from them. Such learning deficiency of evidential models limits their extension to challenging settings. In contrast, the standard model easily overfits the 4 training examples and achieves 100% accuracy.

Visualization of the zero-evidence phenomenon within the toy dataset reveals that two training samples persistently receive zero total evidence throughout the training process. The standard softmax-trained model, facing no analogous constraint, readily overfits the minimal training set to attain perfect accuracy. This stark contrast underscores how the learning deficiency of evidential models fundamentally restricts their scalability to more demanding classification settings.

The generalization performance of evidential models is highly sensitive to the regularization strength. When strong regularization is used, the model focuses strongly on minimizing the incorrect evidence. Such regularization causes the model to push many training samples into or close to the zero-evidence regions, which hurts the model's learning capabilities.

Evidential model generalization is highly susceptible to the magnitude of the incorrect evidence regularization coefficient. Excessively strong regularization compels the model to concentrate almost exclusively on suppressing incorrect evidence, inadvertently driving training samples into proximity with the zero-evidence region. This unintended consequence severely compromises the model's learning capacity by removing large portions of the training set from the effective learning distribution.

Exp activation to transform network outputs into evidence leads to superior performance compared to ReLU and Softplus based transformations. Furthermore, our proposed model with correct evidence regularization further improves over the exp-based evidential models as it enables the evidential model to continue learning from zero-evidence samples.

Exponential activation consistently yields superior classification performance compared to both ReLU and SoftPlus activation functions for evidence transformation. The RED model's additional correct-evidence regularization achieves further gains beyond the exponential activation baseline by specifically enabling the model to extract knowledge from zero-evidence training instances that would otherwise be entirely disregarded.

The proposed RED model has the lowest number of samples in very low evidence regions. Only 0.06% of total training dataset compared to 58.96% of SoftPlus based, and 100% of ReLU based evidential models have very low evidence. This further confirms the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

The sample-wise curve is the function of the number of training samples for a fixed learner. That is, the sample-wise curve is a sequence of performances, one for each training size.

Many learning algorithms implement an iterative internal optimisation process, which allows describing the learning progress over time or a number of iterations. For example, neural network training produces a new hypothesis after every batch or epoch.

A substantial proportion of contemporary learning algorithms are architected around an iterative internal optimization mechanism, which renders it feasible to characterize the progression of learning as a function of elapsed processing cycles. Iteration-wise curves show how much the learner can make out of a constant number of training instances. Instead, sample-wise curves show the performance of the learner as the number of examples grows.

The central epistemic distinction between the two curve modalities lies in what each measures: iteration-wise curves illuminate the extent to which a learner can exploit a fixed corpus through repeated exposure, whereas sample-wise curves chronicle performance improvements attributable to the incremental expansion of the available training set.

Since iterative learners typically automatically stop the learning process as soon as no progress is observed, it often holds that the sample-wise curve value equals the limit of the iteration-wise curve as iterations go to infinity.

Owing to the self-terminating behavior of most iterative algorithms, which cease optimization upon detecting stagnation in progress, the sample-wise performance at a given training size frequently coincides with the asymptotic limit of the corresponding iteration-wise curve as the iteration count tends toward infinity.

To compute learning curves in practice, we rely on empirical estimates of the above quantities. We estimate the out-of-sample error by the internal error, where the dataset used for assessing performance may or may not contain instances used to create the hypothesis.

Owing to the theoretical intractability of computing true learning curve values directly, practitioners must resort to empirical approximations. We consider an empirical learning curve any set of estimates of a true learning curve for different sizes or iterations. We can use various estimation procedures to estimate the performance using a given training size, such as using a regular holdout set or cross-validation.

An empirical learning curve is operationally defined as any collection of performance estimates corresponding to a true learning curve, enumerated across a discrete set of training sizes or iteration counts. The concept of learning curves can be further generalised to a utility curve. The utility usually involves a trade-off between the performance and the computational cost of training a model.

Assuming there is a linear cost associated with further training the classifier, we can see that the utility curve peaks at a given point, and deteriorates afterwards.

The saturation point is the anchor after which the performance convergences. That is, the anchor after which all values are in a distance of less than some pre-defined and typically very small epsilon.

The saturation performance is operationally defined as the performance value attained by the learning curve precisely at the saturation point, representing the practically achievable asymptotic performance level for the given learner and data configuration within the prescribed epsilon-convergence criterion.

A learning curve model is a characterisation of the true learning curve derived from an empirical learning curve. The empirical learning curve is the result of sampling from a stochastic process that underlies noise stemming from randomness in data splits and the learning algorithm itself.

During this process of building a learning curve model, one generally needs to cope with two types of uncertainty. The construction of a learning curve model necessitates confronting two ontologically distinct categories of uncertainty. Epistemic uncertainty, by contrast, pertains to the model's residual ignorance about the true mean performance, a deficiency that can in principle be remedied through the accumulation of additional observations.

The simplest type of learning curve model for a learner just estimates the mean curve values for any possible budget and ignores uncertainty aspects. A considerable number of different parametric models have been proposed over time for this task.

It has been recognised that incorporating some notion of uncertainty into the model itself is important. Formally, this amounts to learn a range estimate function such that for each budget value it produces a bounded interval.

In a more ambitious case, we can try to learn a full belief model of the learning curve. As with the previous approaches, one typically uses parametric functions as a basis but specifies distributions over their parameters instead of a single maximum likelihood assignment.

The most epistemically ambitious approach entails constructing a comprehensive probabilistic belief model over the entire learning curve, wherein distributional specifications over the model's parameters — rather than single maximum-likelihood point assignments — propagate through to induce a full probability measure over the space of plausible learning curve realizations.

Clearly, distribution estimates are the most flexible way of modelling uncertainty and allow many interesting operations. In particular, one can quantify the probability that the limit performance of a learning curve will be above or below some threshold, which is very useful for confidence-based early discarding.

Distribution estimates represent the most expressive and analytically versatile form of uncertainty quantification for learning curve modeling. Federated learning (FL) aims to overcome the challenges of data sharing by enabling collaborative training, which does not require that the involved parties share their training data.

The central server orchestrates the collaborative training process as follows: the initial model is distributed amongst all entities, each entity performs a training iteration on their local model using their own training data, the server averages the model parameters shared by all entities and distributes the resulting model amongst all entities.

After sending an initial model to every participating entity, the central server coordinates the learning cycle: each entity locally refines the model using its own data, then submits its updated parameters; the server aggregates these updates by averaging and redistributes the improved global model back to all participants.

Differential Privacy has its origins in statistical analysis of databases. Its main aim is to address the paradox of learning nothing about specific individuals, while learning useful information about the general population.

Homomorphic Encryption refers to the conversion of plaintext into ciphertext while preserving the structure of the data. Consequently, specific operations applied to the ciphertext will provide the same results as if they were applied to the plaintext but without compromising the encryption.

The defining property of Homomorphic Encryption is that it transforms plaintext data into an encrypted ciphertext form in a manner that preserves structural relationships, allowing computations performed on the ciphertext to yield the exact same outcomes as those performed on the original plaintext, all without ever breaking the encryption.

The plaintext data is never accessed nor decrypted as the operations are directly applied to the encrypted data. The result of the transformations on the ciphertext can only be decrypted back to plaintext by the encryption key owner.

Because all computations are carried out directly on the encrypted form of the data, the underlying plaintext is never exposed or decrypted during processing. Only the holder of the appropriate decryption key can eventually recover the original plaintext from the transformed ciphertext.
