In each temporal computation step, all feasible graph operations are applied to the contemporary internal state of the network, generating a successor state that propagates information forward in time. Unlike feedforward architectures wherein computational layers impose a natural sequential ordering, recurrent neural networks discard the layer concept entirely due to their cyclic graph structure, necessitating a time-step-based computational paradigm that more delicately manages the ordering of operations.

For deep FC NNs, the number of trainable parameters scales like the square of the number of neurons. Pruning techniques seek to reduce the number of parameters or extract sparse subnetworks without affecting the output much.

In standard fully connected architectures, the total parameter count scales quadratically with the neuron count, imposing substantial computational and memory overheads. This has motivated the development of pruning methodologies and sparse subnetwork extraction techniques that aspire to maintain predictive fidelity while dramatically reducing the effective model complexity and associated computational resource requirements.

In addition to playing games, deep learning has also led to impressive breakthroughs in the natural sciences, including drug development, molecular dynamics, and high-energy physics. One of the most astounding breakthroughs is the development of a predictor for protein folding that matches the accuracy of lab-based methods.

Beyond the realm of game-playing, deep learning methodologies have catalyzed transformative breakthroughs across the natural sciences, with documented applications spanning pharmaceutical drug discovery, atomistic molecular dynamics simulation, and high-energy physics experimentation. Among the most extraordinary scientific achievements attributable to deep learning is the construction of a protein structure prediction system achieving accuracy levels commensurate with expensive laboratory-based experimental determination techniques.

The Schrödinger equation describes the stationary nonrelativistic behavior of a quantum mechanical electron system. Its numerical solution is required to obtain stable molecular configurations, compute vibrational spectra, and obtain forces governing molecular dynamics.

The electronic Schrödinger equation governs the stationary, nonrelativistic quantum mechanical behavior of multi-electron molecular systems. Obtaining its numerical solutions is prerequisite for determining energetically stable molecular configurations, computing vibrational spectral properties, and characterizing the force fields governing the dynamical motions of constituent nuclei in molecular simulation frameworks.

Deep-learning based approaches have been very successful in solving a vast array of different partial differential equation models, especially in the high-dimensional regime where most other methods would suffer from the curse of dimensionality.

Neural network-based numerical methodologies have demonstrated remarkable efficacy across a broad spectrum of partial differential equation models, achieving particular distinction in high-dimensional regimes where classical grid-based computational approaches—including finite element methods, sparse grid techniques, and spectral methods—are rendered computationally intractable by the exponential scaling of the curse of dimensionality.

The generalization puzzle refers to the mismatch between predictions of classical theory and the practical generalization of deep NNs. Classical uniform bounds may only deliver insufficient explanation for the observed generalization behavior of overparametrized models.

The generalization puzzle denotes the profound discrepancy between the pessimistic generalization bounds predicted by classical statistical learning theory and the empirically observed generalization capacity of heavily overparametrized deep neural networks. Classical uniform convergence bounds, while theoretically rigorous, appear fundamentally insufficient as explanatory mechanisms for the benign generalization behavior exhibited by modern overparametrized neural architectures.

The question of why stochastic gradient descent converges to good solutions despite the non-convexity of the empirical risk is one of the central open problems. The spin glass analogy suggests that local minima at high loss values are unstable, while those near the global minimum are stable.

The theoretical question of why stochastic gradient descent reliably converges to high-quality solutions despite the severe non-convexity of the training objective constitutes one of the most actively investigated open problems in mathematical deep learning theory. The statistical physics analogy with spin glass models provides partial insight, suggesting through the index-loss distribution that local minima situated at high loss values are energetically unstable, while those in proximity to the global minimum exhibit thermodynamic stability.

For the approximation of Sobolev-regular functions, deep ReLU networks can achieve a rate of epsilon to the power of minus d over k log of 1 over epsilon parameters. This rate matches the optimal rate for classical approximation methods.

For the approximation of functions in Sobolev regularity classes, deep rectified linear unit networks are capable of achieving approximation rates wherein the required parameter count scales as epsilon to the negative d-over-k power multiplied by a logarithmic correction factor, where d denotes the input dimension and k the regularity order. This rate precisely matches the minimax optimal scaling achievable by classical approximation-theoretic methodologies.

The manifold assumption resolves the curse of dimensionality by observing that if data is concentrated on a low-dimensional manifold, then the approximation problem has effective dimension equal to the manifold dimension, not the ambient dimension.

The manifold hypothesis resolves the apparent paradox of successful high-dimensional learning by recognizing that when the data-generating distribution is concentrated on a d-prime dimensional manifold embedded within a higher-dimensional ambient space, the effective approximation-theoretic dimensionality of the problem is determined by d-prime rather than the nominally larger ambient dimension, eliminating the exponential curse.
Computational physics plays a fundamental role in solving many problems in fields of science and engineering.
In the domains of science and engineering, computational physics serves as a cornerstone methodology for tackling a wide array of complex problems.
Based on the observations, postulate a physical law. For instance, you observe that the mass of fluid in a closed system is conserved for all time.

Conservation principles emerge from careful observation — noticing, for example, that the total fluid mass within an isolated system remains invariant across time leads to the formulation of a governing physical law.

In most scenarios, exact expressions of the solution cannot be obtained and must be suitably approximated using a numerical algorithm. For instance, one could use forward or backward Euler, mid-point rule, or Runge-Kutta schemes for solving systems of ODEs.

Runge-Kutta schemes, forward Euler, the mid-point rule, and backward Euler are among the numerical algorithms employed when analytical solutions are unavailable and approximation becomes necessary — a situation that arises in the vast majority of practical scenarios involving ODEs.

Unlike computational physics, machine learning does not require the postulation of a physical law. The general steps involve collecting data, training a suitable algorithm, and using the trained model to make future predictions.

The workflow of machine learning diverges from classical physics-based approaches: rather than deriving governing equations, one collects observational data, fits a learning algorithm to uncover latent patterns, and subsequently deploys that trained model to forecast unseen outcomes.

Supervised learning: Given the data, predict the output for some new input. For instance, given a set of images and image labels, train a classification algorithm to learn the relation between images and labels.

In supervised learning, labeled input-output pairs drive the training process — a paradigmatic example being image classification, where a model learns to associate visual content with categorical labels and then generalizes that mapping to previously unseen images.

Reinforcement learning methods learn driven by rewards or penalties for decisions taken. Thus, a suitable path or policy is learned to maximize the reward. These methods are used to train algorithms to play chess or Go.

Policy optimization through reward signals defines reinforcement learning: an agent accrues positive or negative feedback based on its actions, iteratively refining its decision-making strategy to maximize cumulative reward — a paradigm successfully applied to board games like chess and Go.
AI refers to a system with human-like intelligence. While ML is a key component of an AI system, there are other ingredients involved. A self-driving car is a prototypical example of AI.

Human-like intelligence in machines constitutes the broad ambition of AI, of which machine learning is one essential ingredient among several others. The autonomous vehicle stands as a canonical illustration of a fully realized AI system.

DL is a subset of ML algorithms. The simplest form of a DL architecture, known as a feedforward network, comprises a number of layers of non-linear transformations applied component-wise to an affine transformation of an intermediate output.

Feedforward networks — the most elementary deep learning architecture — stack multiple layers, each applying a component-wise nonlinear function atop an affine transformation of the preceding layer's output. Deep learning itself constitutes a specialized subset within the broader machine learning landscape.

ML in general is very data hungry. But the knowledge of physics can help restrict the manifold on which the input and solution predictions lie. With such constraints, we can reduce the amount of data required to train the ML algorithm.

Physics-informed constraints can substantially alleviate the data demands of machine learning: by confining inputs and predictions to physically plausible manifolds, the volume of training samples required to achieve adequate generalization is markedly reduced.

Computing units of an MLP, called artificial neurons, are stacked in a number of consecutive layers. The zeroth layer is called the source layer, which is not a computing layer but is only responsible for providing an input to the network.

An MLP organizes artificial neurons into a sequence of consecutive layers — the first of which, termed the source layer, performs no computation but simply feeds the raw input signal into the subsequent processing stages.

The last layer of the network is known as the output layer, which outputs the network's prediction. Every other layer in between is known as a hidden layer. The number of neurons in a layer defines the width of that layer.

Sandwiched between the input source and the predictive output layer lie the hidden layers, whose neuron counts determine each layer's width and collectively shape the representational capacity of the entire network.

In each layer, the i-th neuron performs an affine transformation on that layer's input followed by a non-linear transformation. The weights and bias are the trainable parameters, while the activation function plays a pivotal role in helping the network represent non-linear complex functions.

Each neuron executes a two-step operation: first an affine mapping parameterized by learnable weights and a bias, then a nonlinear activation. This activation function is indispensable — without it, the network collapses to a mere linear transformation incapable of capturing complex relationships.
The activation function is perhaps the most important component of an MLP. A large number of activations are available in literature, each with its own advantages and disadvantages.

Among all constituents of a multilayer perceptron, the activation function arguably carries the greatest influence on network behavior. Numerous variants have been proposed in the literature, each exhibiting a distinctive combination of strengths and limitations.

The ReLU function is one of the most popular activation functions used in practice. The function is continuous, while its derivative will be piecewise constant with a jump at zero. The range of the function is zero to infinity.

Piecewise linearity and a range restricted to non-negative values characterize ReLU, whose derivative is piecewise constant with a discontinuity at the origin. Despite these mild irregularities, ReLU enjoys widespread adoption as a default activation choice in practice.

The ReLU activation leads to a null output from a neuron if the affine transformation of the neuron is negative. This can lead to the phenomenon of dying neurons while training a neural network, where neurons drop out completely from the network.

When a neuron's pre-activation value turns negative, ReLU clamps its output to zero — a behavior that, sustained across training, may render entire neurons permanently inactive, a pathology commonly described as the dying neuron phenomenon.
To overcome this challenge, a leaky version of ReLU was designed, where for negative inputs the function outputs a small fraction alpha times the input, where alpha becomes a network hyper-parameter.

Leaky ReLU addresses neuronal death by permitting a small, scaled response even for negative pre-activation values; the scaling coefficient alpha is treated as a tunable hyperparameter rather than a fixed constant.

The Logistic or Sigmoid activation function is infinitely smooth and monotonic. The range of the function is between zero and one, making it useful in representing probabilities. Since the derivative quickly decays to zero away from the origin, this activation function can lead to slow convergence.

Smoothness, monotonicity, and an output bounded within the unit interval make the sigmoid well-suited for probabilistic interpretation. However, its derivative's rapid decay toward zero in the saturation regions tends to impede gradient flow and slow down network convergence during training.

Recently, the sine function has been proposed as an efficient activation function. It has the best features of all the activation functions discussed: the function is infinitely smooth, its range is bounded, and none of the derivatives of this function decay to zero.

The sine activation combines the most desirable properties of other activations: infinite differentiability, a bounded output range, and — crucially — derivatives that never vanish, eliminating the gradient saturation issues that plague sigmoid-like functions.

The expressivity of a network grows as the depth and width increase. For ReLU networks, the number of kinks in the output can grow as H to the power L, where H is the width and L is the depth of the network.

Network expressivity scales dramatically with architecture: in ReLU networks, the number of representable piecewise-linear segments — quantified by kink count — can grow exponentially as H raised to the L, where H denotes layer width and L the network depth.

The universal approximation theorem states that given any continuous function and any epsilon greater than zero, there exists an MLP with a single hidden layer of arbitrary width and a non-polynomial continuous activation such that the maximum error is less than epsilon.

A foundational result in neural network theory guarantees that a single hidden layer of sufficient width, equipped with any non-polynomial continuous activation, can approximate an arbitrary continuous function to within any prescribed error tolerance epsilon.

Splitting the dataset is necessary as neural networks are heavily over-parameterized functions. The large number of degrees of freedom can lead to over-fitting, where the error or noise present in the data drives the behavior of the network more than the underlying input-output relation.

Over-parameterization renders neural networks susceptible to overfitting, a regime where the model latches onto noise and idiosyncrasies in the training data rather than capturing the true underlying relationship — motivating the partitioning of available data into disjoint training, validation, and test subsets.
Training the network involves solving an optimization problem using the training set to find the optimal weights that minimize the mean-squared loss function over all training samples.

The training phase frames parameter estimation as an optimization problem: the network weights are adjusted iteratively to minimize the average squared discrepancy between predicted and target outputs across all training examples.

Validation of the network involves using the validation set to find the optimal hyper-parameters such as depth, width, and type of activation function. The optimal hyper-parameters are obtained using techniques such as random or tensor grid search.

Hyperparameter selection — governing choices such as network depth, layer width, and activation type — is performed on the held-out validation set, typically via grid search or random search strategies that explore the hyperparameter space systematically.
Neural networks, especially MLPs, are almost always over-parametrized. This would lead to a highly non-linear network model for which the loss function can have a landscape with many local minima.

The loss landscape of an over-parametrized MLP is highly non-convex, riddled with numerous local minima — an inherent consequence of the model's vastly greater number of trainable parameters relative to the number of available training points.

The simplest method of regularization involves augmenting a penalty term to the loss function. This encourages the selection of a minimum corresponding to smaller values of the parameters, which in turn reduces the network's sensitivity to small changes in the input.

Adding a norm penalty to the training objective steers the optimizer toward parameter configurations with smaller magnitudes, thereby reducing the network's sensitivity to perturbations in the input and mitigating the risk of overfitting to training-specific noise.
L2 regularization uses the L2 norm in the regularization term, while L1 regularization uses the L1 norm, which promotes the sparsity of the parameters.

The L2 penalty shrinks all parameters uniformly, whereas the L1 variant encourages sparse parameter vectors by driving many weights exactly to zero — a property with useful implications for feature selection and model interpretability.

Gradient descent works by choosing the step in the opposite direction of the gradient, with the step-size also known as the learning rate. The convergence assumes the loss function is convex and differentiable with a Lipschitz continuous gradient.

Steepest descent iterates by moving opposite to the local gradient, with the step magnitude controlled by the learning rate. Under the assumptions of convexity and Lipschitz continuity of the gradient, convergence is guaranteed at a rate inversely proportional to iteration count.

Gradient descent prefers to converge to a minima with a flat or small curvature. There is empirical evidence that parameter values obtained at flat minima tend to generalize better and are therefore to be preferred.

Flat minima are preferentially selected by gradient descent due to its implicit bias toward low-curvature regions. Empirical studies consistently show that parameters residing at flat minima exhibit superior generalization to unseen data compared to those at sharp minima.

Momentum methods make use of the history of the gradient, instead of just the gradient at the previous step. The formula computes a weighted moving average of the gradient, which is expected to smooth out the zig-zagging behavior.

By maintaining a running exponential average of past gradients, momentum-based optimizers accumulate directional inertia that suppresses oscillatory zig-zag trajectories and accelerates convergence — especially in loss landscapes featuring elongated ravines.

The Adam optimization makes use of the history of the gradient as well as the second moment of the gradient, which is a measure of the magnitude. The learning rate for each component is different — components with larger gradient magnitudes receive smaller learning rates.

Adam adapts per-parameter learning rates by tracking both the first-order gradient history and the second moment (uncentered variance): parameters whose gradients tend to be large are assigned smaller effective step sizes, while those with historically small gradients receive larger ones.

In stochastic gradient descent, the gradient is approximated using only a single randomly chosen training sample at each update step. This modified algorithm does converge assuming the loss function is convex and the learning rate decays as one over the square root of the iteration count.

SGD approximates the true gradient using a single randomly drawn sample per update, dramatically reducing per-iteration computational cost. Convergence is maintained provided the learning rate schedule decays at the appropriate rate — typically proportional to the reciprocal square root of the iteration index.

Mini-batch optimization is a compromise between full-batch and single-sample stochastic gradient descent. The dataset is split into disjoint subsets called mini-batches, and the gradient is approximated using the samples within each mini-batch.

Mini-batch training strikes a balance between the stability of full-batch gradient descent and the computational efficiency of single-sample SGD: the gradient estimate is computed over a small, randomly drawn subset of the training data, enabling efficient use of hardware parallelism while maintaining reasonable gradient quality.

Back-propagation works by first performing a forward pass to evaluate all intermediate hidden variables and the loss function, then traversing the computational graph in reverse to evaluate gradients using the chain rule.

The chain rule applied in reverse along the computational graph constitutes backpropagation: intermediate activations are first computed during a forward sweep, then gradient signals are propagated backwards from the loss, accumulating contributions layer by layer.

For classification problems, the softmax function is used as an output function to transform the network's output vector into a valid probability vector, where each component lies between zero and one and the components sum to one.

Softmax normalizes the raw output logits into a proper probability distribution: each element is exponentiated and divided by the sum of all exponentiated values, ensuring non-negativity and a unit sum — the prerequisites for a valid categorical probability vector.

The cross-entropy loss function is preferred for classification problems. It severely penalizes strongly confident incorrect predictions. As the predicted probability for the wrong class approaches one, the cross-entropy loss approaches infinity, unlike the MSE which approaches a finite value.

Cross-entropy diverges to infinity as the model confidently assigns near-unit probability to an incorrect class, imposing a far harsher penalty than the mean squared error, which remains bounded even at maximum misclassification confidence. This asymmetry makes cross-entropy the preferred loss for classification.

Residual networks were introduced to address the problem of vanishing gradients in deep networks. When the weights of the network approach small values, a standard deep network approaches the null mapping, whereas a ResNet approaches the identity mapping.

The core innovation of ResNets lies in shifting the network's default behavior from the null mapping to the identity: when weights become small, skip connections ensure that the output simply passes through unchanged, circumventing the vanishing gradient pathology that plagues very deep standard networks.

The problem of vanishing gradients manifests itself in deep networks where the weights in the inner layers do not contribute to the network. This typically happens when the depth minus the current layer exceeds approximately twenty.

At depths beyond roughly twenty layers from the output, gradient magnitudes become negligibly small through successive matrix multiplications, effectively decoupling the corresponding weights from the training signal and rendering those layers unable to learn.

In a ResNet, skip connections are added between hidden layers such that the output of a layer is the sum of the standard activation and the input to that layer. This ensures that even when all weights are null, the gradient near the input layer is not significantly different from the gradient near the output layer.

Skip connections in ResNets additively combine each layer's standard output with its input: a zeroed-weight scenario then reduces to an identity pass-through, and the consequent gradient flow carries the output-layer signal back to the input layer without multiplicative attenuation.

A ResNet can be seen as a discretization of a nonlinear system of ODEs. The skip connection update rule is analogous to a forward Euler time-integration scheme, where the layer index plays the role of the discrete time variable.

Interpreting the layer index as a discrete time variable, each ResNet residual block enacts a forward Euler integration step for a nonlinear ODE — the network depth thus corresponds to the number of time steps, and the learned transformation at each block approximates the ODE's right-hand side.

In a Neural ODE, the right-hand side of the ODE system is defined using a feed-forward neural network. The system is then solved using a suitable time-marching scheme such as forward Euler or Runge-Kutta, and the regression problem becomes one of finding the RHS that maps initial points to final points.

Neural ODEs recast supervised learning as an initial value problem: a neural network parameterizes the ODE's right-hand side, an off-the-shelf ODE solver propagates initial states to their terminal values, and training adjusts the network weights so that those terminal values align with the target outputs.

A key advantage of Neural ODEs over ResNets is that the number of weights is independent of the number of time steps used to solve the ODE. This means one can take the limit of small time steps and study convergence without changing the network size.

Unlike ResNets, whose parameter count grows linearly with depth, Neural ODEs decouple network size from integration resolution: the same network represents the ODE's vector field regardless of how finely the time axis is discretized, enabling principled convergence analysis as the step size shrinks toward zero.

The finite difference method discretizes the domain into a grid of points, approximates derivatives with finite difference formulas, and reduces the PDE to a system of algebraic equations that can be solved with standard linear algebra techniques.

Finite difference schemes transform a continuous PDE into a discrete algebraic system by replacing derivative operators with weighted combinations of nearby grid values, ultimately yielding a matrix equation whose solution approximates the PDE solution at the grid nodes.

Physics-informed neural networks use a neural network to represent the solution of a PDE, and define a loss function containing the PDE residual evaluated at a set of collocation points in the interior of the domain and boundary residual terms.

PINNs embed the physics directly into the training objective: the network output is substituted into the PDE and boundary conditions, and the resulting residuals evaluated at scattered collocation points are penalized in the loss — eliminating the need for a mesh while retaining physical fidelity.

A key property of PINNs is that derivatives of the network output with respect to its input can be evaluated using back-propagation, enabling the PDE residuals to be computed automatically through automatic differentiation frameworks.

Automatic differentiation through back-propagation furnishes exact partial derivatives of the network output with respect to its spatial and temporal inputs, making it straightforward to assemble PDE residuals without finite differencing or manual derivation.

The boundary conditions in PINNs are enforced as a soft constraint via a penalization term weighted by a hyper-parameter lambda. Proper scaling of this hyper-parameter is crucial, especially for stiff PDEs, and self-adaptive techniques have been proposed to tune it during training.

Rather than hard-coding boundary conditions into the network architecture, PINNs penalize boundary violations through a weighted loss term. The weighting coefficient lambda demands careful calibration — imbalanced gradient scales can severely retard convergence, motivating adaptive schemes that automatically adjust lambda during optimization.

The error analysis for PINNs shows that the solution error is bounded by a term that decreases as the number of network parameters increases and by terms that decrease as the number of interior and boundary collocation points increases.

Formal error bounds for PINNs reveal a two-pronged convergence mechanism: increasing the network's parameter count reduces the approximation component of the error, while densifying the collocation point sets reduces the quadrature-type discretization error in the loss.

Spectral collocation methods seek a solution written as an expansion in terms of a set of smooth and global basis functions. The coefficients of the expansion are unknowns, computed by requiring that the numerical solution of the PDE is exact at a set of collocation points.

In spectral collocation, the unknown PDE solution is expanded in a pre-selected global basis — such as Chebyshev polynomials — and the expansion coefficients are determined by enforcing the PDE exactly at a discrete set of collocation points, yielding a linear or nonlinear algebraic system.

The convolution operator maps functions to functions by sampling one function using a sliding kernel. As the kernel shifts to different locations, it samples the input function in different windows, but the same operation is applied regardless of location.

Spatial translation equivariance defines the convolution operator: a kernel slides across the domain, sampling the input function within a local window at each position while applying an identical operation everywhere — a property that makes convolution naturally suited to spatially homogeneous tasks.

The Gaussian kernel is a popular choice for convolution and is used as a smoothing or blurring filter. It is isotropic, its integral over the whole domain is unity, and it filters out scales finer than the parameter sigma.

Isotropic and unit-normalized, the Gaussian kernel acts as a low-pass filter: spatial features finer than the characteristic scale sigma are attenuated by convolution, yielding a smoothed version of the input while preserving large-scale structure.

In a convolution layer, the weights of the kernel are learnable parameters determined during training. The network thus learns the operations — smoothing, edge detection, differentiation — that are appropriate for its task.

Convolution kernels are not handcrafted but discovered through gradient-based optimization: training adapts the kernel weights so that the layer learns whatever local operation — be it smoothing, gradient estimation, or feature detection — proves most useful for the downstream task.

Pooling operations are used to reduce the size of an image. Max pooling takes the maximum value over patches of a specified size, while average pooling takes the mean. These operations have no trainable parameters.

Spatial downsampling via pooling requires no learnable parameters: max pooling extracts the dominant activation within each non-overlapping patch, while average pooling computes the mean — both reducing spatial resolution and introducing a degree of translation invariance.

In a CNN for image classification, convolution layers encode information about the input image through feature selection, while the fully connected layers use this encoded information to solve the classification problem. The convolution portion is often referred to as the encoder.

The encoder-classifier duality in CNNs assigns distinct roles to each architectural segment: convolutional layers progressively extract and compress spatial features into a compact representation, which fully connected layers then decode into class-probability outputs.

Transpose convolution layers perform the inverse operation of standard convolutions: instead of using a dot product, they use an outer product; instead of skipping pixels in the input via stride, they skip pixels in the output.

Upsampling through transpose convolutions inverts the arithmetic of standard convolutions — outer products replace inner products, and the stride governs gaps in the output rather than in the input, enabling learned spatial upscaling from coarse feature maps.

Checker-boarding is an undesirable artifact of transpose convolution that arises when the filter size is not an integer multiple of the stride, causing output pixels to receive unequal contributions from different patches.

When the kernel size and stride are incommensurable, different output pixels accumulate contributions from different numbers of input patches, producing a periodic amplitude modulation — the checker-board artifact — that degrades image quality in the transposed convolution output.

U-Nets have a downward branch that downscales images using convolution and pooling, and an upward branch that upscales using transpose convolutions. Skip connections combine information at matching spatial scales across the two branches.

The U-Net's symmetric encoder-decoder structure is augmented by lateral skip connections that concatenate feature maps of identical spatial resolution from the contracting path to the expanding path, preserving fine-grained spatial detail that would otherwise be lost during downsampling.

The U-net architecture shares many common features with the V-cycle used in multigrid preconditioners. It can also be thought of as an encoder-decoder network with the additional feature of including skip connections.

Multigrid V-cycle hierarchies and U-Net architectures share a deep structural analogy: both traverse from fine to coarse scales and back, leveraging information across resolutions — the primary distinction being that U-Nets learn their inter-scale transformations from data rather than from prescribed prolongation and restriction operators.

PINNs have a fundamental limitation: the trained network corresponds to a single instance of the PDE for specific boundary conditions and source terms. If any of these change, the network must be retrained from scratch.

Each PINN training run encodes the solution for one specific configuration of source terms and boundary conditions; altering either necessitates a full retraining cycle, making PINNs poorly suited for parametric studies or scenarios requiring solutions across a family of related PDEs.

Operator networks are designed to approximate operators that map functions to functions, rather than simply mapping a finite-dimensional input vector to an output vector as standard neural networks do.

Standard networks map vectors to vectors, but many physical problems demand mappings between infinite-dimensional function spaces. Operator networks generalize deep learning to this setting, learning to approximate the functional relationships that connect input functions to output functions.

A DeepONet comprises two sub-networks: a branch net that encodes the input function sampled at fixed sensor points, and a trunk net that encodes the output query location. Their outputs are combined via a dot product to produce the predicted solution value.

The DeepONet architecture decomposes operator learning into two parallel streams: the branch network digests discrete samples of the input function at pre-specified sensor locations, the trunk network processes the spatial query point, and a final dot product merges these representations into a scalar output.

The DeepONet output can be interpreted as a generalized basis expansion: the trunk network generates data-driven basis functions, while the branch network computes the corresponding coefficients that depend on the input function.

DeepONet's dot-product output formula mirrors a basis expansion: the trunk network's outputs serve as learned, data-adapted basis functions over the output domain, while the branch network's outputs furnish the associated expansion coefficients — coefficients that implicitly encode the entire input function.

Training a DeepONet requires pairwise data: representative input functions are sampled at sensor points, the corresponding output functions are computed numerically or analytically, and those outputs are sampled at query points to form the training set.

The supervised training pipeline for DeepONets assembles input-output function pairs: input functions are evaluated at fixed sensor nodes to form the branch network's input vectors, reference output functions are computed via external solvers and sampled at query locations, and the combined dataset drives parameter optimization.

Physics-Informed DeepONets augment the standard data-driven loss with a physics-based loss that penalizes PDE residuals at additional collocation points. This reduces the data demand and improves robustness to out-of-distribution input functions.

By supplementing data-driven supervision with a PDE-residual penalty evaluated at physics collocation points, physics-informed DeepONets transfer some of the learning burden from expensive labeled data to the governing equations — improving both sample efficiency and generalization beyond the training distribution.

Fourier Neural Operators extend the standard MLP architecture from scalars to functions by replacing vector-to-vector affine transforms with function-to-function operators that include a convolution term in addition to the pointwise affine transformation.

FNOs generalize the MLP computational graph to infinite-dimensional function spaces: each hidden layer now transforms vector-valued functions rather than finite vectors, with the affine operator augmented by an integral convolution term that captures global dependencies across the spatial domain.

The convolution in the Fourier Neural Operator is computed efficiently using the Fast Fourier Transform. By transforming to the Fourier domain, multiplying coefficients, and inverting, the cost of the convolution reduces from order N squared H squared to order N log N H squared.

Leveraging the FFT's O(N log N) complexity, FNOs bypass the quadratic cost of direct spatial convolution: the input function's Fourier coefficients are multiplied pointwise by learned spectral filters, and the inverse FFT reconstructs the convolved function — a pipeline that scales gracefully with spatial resolution.

In probabilistic deep learning, the output for a given input is not a single value but a distribution. This framework is necessary when outputs are inherently stochastic, measurements are noisy, or inverse problems admit multiple solutions.

Deterministic networks are inadequate for settings where the mapping from input to output is one-to-many: measurement noise, intrinsic randomness, and ill-posed inverse problems all demand a probabilistic treatment in which the network characterizes an entire conditional distribution rather than a single point estimate.

A random variable is a function defined from the sample space to the real line. Its probabilistic interpretation is inherited from the probability law defined on the sample space through the assignment of probabilities to events.

Formally, a random variable is a measurable mapping from the underlying probability space to the real line, acquiring its probabilistic character from the probability measure defined on the original sample space via the induced distribution over real-valued outcomes.

The cumulative distribution function of a random variable X gives the probability that X takes a value less than or equal to x. It is always monotonically non-decreasing, bounded between zero and one, and right-continuous.

The CDF encodes the complete distributional information of a random variable: evaluated at any threshold x, it returns the probability of falling at or below that value. Its defining properties — monotone non-decrease, unit-limit at infinity, and right-continuity — follow directly from the axioms of probability.

The probability density function is defined as the derivative of the cumulative distribution function. The integral of the pdf over an interval gives the probability mass, which is the probability that the random variable lies in that interval.

Differentiating the CDF yields the pdf, whose integral over any interval computes the probability that the random variable falls within that range — making the pdf interpretable as a probability mass density in the limit of infinitesimally small intervals.

The Gaussian random variable is parameterized by its mean, which denotes the center of the distribution, and its variance, which denotes the spread. Through the Central Limit Theorem, it also arises as the limiting distribution of aggregates of many independent random variables.

Mean and variance fully characterize the Gaussian distribution: the former locates the distribution's center while the latter governs its width. The Central Limit Theorem endows this distribution with universal significance — sums of sufficiently many independent random variables, regardless of their individual distributions, converge to Gaussian in the limit.

Generative Adversarial Networks comprise two sub-networks: a generator that maps samples from a simple latent distribution to the data space, and a critic or discriminator that attempts to distinguish real data samples from generated fake samples.

The GAN framework pits two networks in opposition: the generator transforms low-dimensional latent noise into synthetic data-space samples, while the critic assigns high scores to genuine data and low scores to generated fakes — the adversarial tension between them driving both networks toward improved performance.

The Wasserstein GAN objective trains the critic to maximize the difference between its average score on real samples and its average score on fake samples. The generator is trained to minimize this same objective, creating a minimax optimization problem.

WGAN frames training as a two-player zero-sum game: the critic maximizes the expected score gap between authentic and synthetic samples, while the generator minimizes it — the Nash equilibrium of this minimax problem theoretically corresponding to the generator reproducing the true data distribution.

A gradient penalty term is added to the critic loss in WGAN to constrain the norm of the critic's gradient with respect to its input to be close to one, enforcing the one-Lipschitz condition required for the Wasserstein distance interpretation.

Enforcing the one-Lipschitz constraint on the critic — a prerequisite for the Wasserstein-1 distance interpretation — is accomplished through a gradient penalty that penalizes deviations of the gradient norm from unity, evaluated at interpolated points between real and generated samples.

Once a GAN is trained, only the generator is retained. Given a latent sample from the simple prior distribution, it produces a new synthetic sample whose statistics converge to those of the true data distribution as training proceeds.

Post-training, the critic is discarded and the generator alone is deployed: sampling a latent vector from the prior and passing it through the trained generator yields a synthetic observation whose marginal distribution approximates the true data distribution — with statistics converging as training quality improves.

Conditional GANs extend standard GANs to the supervised setting by conditioning the generator on an observed input x in addition to the latent variable z. The goal is to approximate the conditional distribution of the output given the input.

cGANs adapt the GAN framework for regression-like tasks: the generator receives both a latent sample and the observed conditioning variable x, producing output samples that collectively approximate the true conditional distribution of the output given that specific input value.

The spectral collocation method can be viewed as a special case of a least-squares approach where the solution is represented as a linear combination of global basis functions and the coefficients are found by minimizing a loss function containing the PDE residual and boundary conditions.

Casting spectral collocation as a least-squares problem unifies it conceptually with neural network PDE solvers: in both cases, a parameterized function space is explored by minimizing a weighted combination of interior PDE residuals and boundary condition violations — the principal difference being the choice of basis functions.

The data assimilation problem involves using sparse measurements of a quantity together with a known physical constraint to reconstruct the field everywhere in the domain. PINNs can solve this by including both a data matching term and a physics residual term in the loss.

Sparse observations and governing physics jointly constrain the solution in data assimilation: PINNs formalize this by optimizing a composite loss that simultaneously penalizes discrepancies from the available measurements and violations of the PDE residual at additional collocation points — effectively interpolating the field in a physically consistent manner.

The error in a DeepONet solution is bounded by terms accounting for the numerical solver accuracy used to generate training data, the final training loss, how well the training functions cover the input space, and quadrature errors from discretizing the input and output functions.

DeepONet error decomposes into four additive contributions: inaccuracy inherited from the numerical solver producing training labels, residual optimization error at convergence, coverage gaps between training function samples and the full input function class, and discretization errors from evaluating functions at finite sensor and output nodes.

The action of the whole network can be mathematically seen as a composition of alternating affine transformations and component-wise activations, applied sequentially from the first layer to the last.

Mathematically, a feedforward network computes a nested composition of alternating linear affine maps and pointwise nonlinear activation functions, progressively transforming the input representation layer by layer until the final output is produced.

For the Yarotsky universal approximation result, if the target function has two continuous derivatives and the network uses ReLU activations with at least a certain minimum width, then the maximum approximation error decays as a power of the total number of network parameters.

Yarotsky's quantitative approximation theorem establishes that ReLU networks of sufficient width can approximate twice-continuously-differentiable functions with an error that decays polynomially in the total parameter count — providing a concrete rate linking network size to approximation quality.

For a network to generalize well, the training set, validation set, and test set should all be drawn from the same data distribution. A small training and validation loss can then be expected to lead to a small testing error.

Distributional consistency across the three data splits is a prerequisite for meaningful generalization guarantees: when all partitions share a common generating distribution, minimizing training and validation loss provides meaningful assurance that the model will perform similarly on held-out test data.

In gradient descent, the convergence rate is bounded by C divided by k, where k is the iteration number and C is a constant. This linear convergence rate holds when the loss function is convex and the gradient is Lipschitz continuous.

Under convexity and Lipschitz gradient assumptions, gradient descent enjoys an O(1/k) convergence rate — the distance to the optimal parameters shrinks inversely with the number of iterations, a rate that, while moderate, carries theoretical guarantees absent in the non-convex setting.

The zig-zagging behavior of gradient descent in elongated loss landscapes can be mitigated by the Adam optimizer, which maintains separate adaptive learning rates for each parameter based on the running averages of the gradient and the squared gradient.

Adam resolves the zig-zag pathology inherent to gradient descent in anisotropic loss landscapes by scaling each parameter's effective learning rate inversely with the root mean square of its recent gradient history, enabling larger steps in flat directions and smaller steps in steep ones.

One epoch in mini-batch stochastic optimization is defined as one full pass through all samples or mini-batches of the full training set. The training algorithm randomly shuffles the full training set and creates mini-batches before processing each one sequentially.

A single epoch constitutes one complete sweep through the training corpus: the data is first shuffled to decorrelate successive mini-batches, then partitioned into equal-sized subsets, each of which contributes one gradient update before the epoch concludes and the next reshuffle begins.

The finite difference method uses central difference approximations that are second order accurate for both the first and second derivatives. In the limit of large Peclet number, a central difference approximation of the advective term is not ideal since it leads to numerical instability.

Central differencing achieves second-order accuracy for spatial derivatives but becomes numerically unstable at high Peclet numbers, where advection dominates diffusion; in that regime, upwind differencing — which biases the stencil in the flow direction — is the preferred alternative.

The solution to the advection-diffusion equation with zero source term involves the Peclet number, which measures the ratio of the strength of advection to the strength of diffusion. For small Peclet number the solution is nearly linear, while for large Peclet number a steep boundary layer forms near one boundary.

As the Peclet number grows, the balance between advective and diffusive transport shifts dramatically: at small values the solution profile is essentially linear, but at large values a thin boundary layer with steep gradients emerges near the downstream boundary, posing challenges for numerical methods.

In the spectral collocation method, Chebyshev polynomials are a natural choice of basis because they form a complete basis, are smooth enough to allow derivative evaluation, are easy to evaluate via a recurrence relation, and have derivatives that are also easy to evaluate.

Chebyshev polynomials satisfy all the desiderata for a spectral basis: completeness in the relevant function space, smoothness enabling repeated differentiation, efficient recursive evaluation, and derivative recurrences that are equally tractable — making them the canonical choice for spectral collocation on bounded intervals.

When a nonlinear PDE is treated by spectral collocation, the result is a nonlinear system of algebraic equations for the basis coefficients, which is typically solved iteratively using Newton's method rather than a direct linear solver.

Nonlinearity in the PDE propagates into the spectral system, replacing the linear coefficient matrix with a nonlinear algebraic residual that must be driven to zero — typically through Newton iteration, which linearizes the system at each step and solves the resulting Jacobian system.

In extending PINNs to the Navier-Stokes equations, the input to the network includes the three spatial coordinates and the time variable, while the output includes the three velocity components and the pressure field.

For the three-dimensional incompressible Navier-Stokes equations, the PINN network accepts a four-dimensional input comprising the spatial coordinates and time, and outputs a four-dimensional vector encoding the velocity field and pressure — with the PDE's momentum balance, mass conservation, and boundary conditions all embedded in the loss.

In the PINN framework, the universal approximation theorems guarantee completeness of the function representation, back-propagation provides derivative evaluation, and the collocation points play the role analogous to the quadrature points in spectral methods.

PINNs inherit their approximation completeness from universal approximation theorems, their derivative evaluation from automatic differentiation, and their discretization strategy from the choice of collocation points — with each of these elements having a direct counterpart in classical spectral collocation methodology.

The operator that maps the right-hand side of a linear PDE to its solution is called the Green's operator. This is an example of a linear operator and motivates the use of convolution in the Fourier Neural Operator architecture.

Green's operators furnish the canonical example of a linear function-to-function map: they express the PDE solution as an integral transform of the forcing function — a convolution structure that directly motivates the integral kernel term incorporated into each layer of the Fourier Neural Operator.

In the DeepONet architecture, when the input function is sampled on a uniform grid, the branch network is best implemented using convolutional layers, since the sensor points form an image-like structure that CNNs are well-suited to process.

Uniform sensor grids endow the branch network's input with a regular spatial structure amenable to convolutional processing: the sampled function values form an image, and convolutional layers can exploit the local spatial correlations among neighboring sensor readings far more efficiently than fully connected layers.

The error estimate for DeepONets is similar in structure to the error estimate for PINNs: both involve terms that can be reduced by increasing the number of network parameters, and both involve discretization error terms that decrease as the number of collocation or sensor points increases.

A structural parallel links the error bounds of PINNs and DeepONets: both decompose into an approximation component shrunk by growing the network and a quadrature component shrunk by densifying the spatial point sets — reflecting the dual role of model capacity and discretization resolution in controlling accuracy.

The marginal probability density function of one random variable in a pair can be obtained by integrating the joint density over all possible values of the other variable. This operation is called marginalization.

Marginalization extracts the distribution of a single variable from a joint distribution by summing — or integrating, in the continuous case — over the entire range of the other variable, collapsing the bivariate density onto a univariate one.

Two random variables are said to be independent if their joint probability density function factors into the product of their individual marginal density functions. Independence implies zero covariance, but zero covariance does not imply independence.

Statistical independence is characterized by the factorization of the joint density into the product of marginals — a strictly stronger condition than zero covariance, which merely captures linear uncorrelatedness but leaves open the possibility of nonlinear stochastic dependence.

The conditional probability density function of Y given X equals the joint density divided by the marginal density of X. This quantity is the foundation of Bayesian inference and probabilistic regression.

Bayes' rule for densities divides the joint probability of the pair by the marginal density of the conditioning variable, yielding the conditional density — the central object in both Bayesian inference and probabilistic regression, encoding all information about the output distribution given a specific input observation.

GANs were first proposed by Goodfellow et al. in 2014. Since then many variants have been proposed differing in network architecture and the objective function used to train the networks. The generator and critic play adversarial roles in training.

Since their introduction by Goodfellow and colleagues in 2014, GANs have spawned a rich family of variants distinguished by architectural choices and training objectives. In all variants, generator and critic interact antagonistically — the former learns to synthesize convincing samples while the latter sharpens its ability to detect them.

The latent variable of a GAN has a much lower dimension than the data space. As a result, the trained generator also provides a low-dimensional representation of high-dimensional data, which can be useful in downstream tasks involving uncertainty quantification.

The dimensionality gap between the low-dimensional latent space and the high-dimensional data manifold means the trained GAN implicitly discovers a compact embedding of the data: this latent representation serves as a learned prior useful for uncertainty quantification and Bayesian inverse problem formulations.

Under the assumptions of infinite network capacity, infinite training data, and a perfect optimizer, it can be proven that the distribution of samples generated by the trained GAN converges weakly to the true target data distribution.

Theoretical guarantees for WGAN training establish weak convergence of the generated distribution to the target under idealized conditions — unlimited model capacity, infinite data, and a globally optimal solver — demonstrating that the adversarial training objective is in principle consistent with the true generative goal.

Conditional Wasserstein GANs are designed to learn conditional distributions. The generator takes both the latent variable and the conditioning input as inputs, and the critic receives paired conditioning input and output samples to distinguish real pairs from fake ones.

cWGANs adapt the Wasserstein framework to conditional distribution learning: the generator's input space is augmented with the conditioning variable, while the critic evaluates joint input-output pairs — assigning high scores to true pairings and low scores to pairs where the output was generated rather than observed.

The FNO architecture is obtained by systematically extending a standard MLP from scalars to scalar-valued functions. Scalar inputs and outputs become function inputs and outputs, finite-dimensional weight vectors become pointwise affine operators, and the affine transform in hidden layers gains an integral convolution term.

FNO construction follows a principled lifting of the MLP graph: scalars become functions, weight matrices become pointwise linear operators, and crucially, each hidden-layer affine step is enriched with an integral convolution — an addition that confers the ability to capture nonlocal, long-range dependencies across the spatial domain.

The use of Fast Fourier Transforms in FNOs reduces the cost of evaluating the convolution from order N squared to order N log N, where N is the number of spatial grid points. This makes the FNO practical for high-resolution problems.

FFT-based evaluation of the spectral convolution achieves sub-quadratic complexity: rather than summing over all N grid-point pairs, the transform-multiply-invert pipeline operates at O(N log N) cost — an efficiency gain that makes FNOs competitive with classical numerical solvers even on high-resolution spatial grids.

The FNO truncates the Fourier series to a finite number of modes, retaining only the lower frequency components and discarding the higher frequency ones. The weights applied to these retained Fourier coefficients are the trainable parameters of the convolution.

Frequency truncation in the FNO limits the learned convolution to a finite-dimensional spectral subspace: only the first K Fourier modes per spatial dimension are retained and multiplied by trainable complex-valued weight tensors, with higher-frequency components set to zero — an implicit regularity assumption on the target operator.

The FNO treats the discretization of the domain as an implementation detail rather than a fundamental limitation, allowing the trained operator to be evaluated at different spatial resolutions without retraining — a property sometimes called discretization invariance.

Resolution invariance distinguishes FNOs from grid-dependent models: because the underlying operator is learned in the continuous Fourier domain, the trained network can be queried at any discretization of the spatial domain without modification, enabling zero-shot generalization to finer or coarser grids.

In the DeepONet, the M sensor points must be pre-defined before training and remain fixed throughout training and evaluation. The branch network encodes only the values of the input function at these fixed sensor locations.

Sensor placement is a design decision made prior to DeepONet training and cannot be changed thereafter: the branch network's input is exclusively the vector of function evaluations at these pre-committed locations, making the choice of sensor points an important hyperparameter affecting representational capacity.

The variance of a uniform random variable on the interval from a to b equals the square of the interval length divided by twelve. The variance of a Gaussian random variable equals the square of the parameter sigma.

For a uniform distribution over an interval of length b minus a, the variance evaluates to the square of that length divided by twelve. The Gaussian distribution's variance is simply sigma squared — the parameter that appears in the exponent of the density's bell-curve formula.
We consider the generic deep image enhancement problem where an input image is transformed into a perceptually better-looking image.

The problem under consideration is the broad challenge of deep image enhancement, wherein the primary objective is to transform a given degraded input image into a visually superior output exhibiting improved perceptual quality as assessed by human observers and quantitative perceptual metrics.

Recent methods for image enhancement consider the problem by performing style transfer and image restoration. The methods mostly fall into two categories: training data-based and training data-independent methods.

Contemporary image enhancement approaches have converged upon two principal methodological paradigms for addressing the enhancement problem: those that frame it through the lens of style transfer combined with image restoration, and those categorized broadly as either requiring curated paired training data or operating independently of such externally sourced supervisory signals.
Deep image enhancement is an ill-posed problem that aims to improve the perceptual quality of an image using a deep neural network.

The task of enhancing images through deep learning constitutes a fundamentally ill-posed inverse problem, wherein a deep neural network serves as the computational instrument for elevating the subjective perceptual fidelity of the processed imagery in the absence of a unique mathematically determined solution.
An image could be considered as the composition of content features and style features. The content features denote the objects, their structure, and their relative positions.

An image may be conceptualized as a superposition of two distinct representational modalities: content features, which encode the semantic inventory of depicted objects alongside their structural configurations and spatial interrelationships, and style features, which capture the chromatic and textural characteristics of the visual scene.
Style features represent the color and the texture information of the objects. Deep image enhancement aims to improve the quality of the content and the style features.

The stylistic dimension of an image is predominantly constituted by its chromatic distribution and the textural properties characterizing its constituent regions. Comprehensive image enhancement therefore necessitates the concurrent amelioration of both the content and the stylistic representational components embedded within the image.

The image features may get corrupted in various ways. For example, bad weather conditions, camera shake, and noise. Consider a hazy image denoted by I. Haze particles degrade both the content features and the style features.

Image features are susceptible to corruption through a diverse array of degradation mechanisms including adverse atmospheric conditions, motion-induced blur, and stochastic sensor noise. Taking a haze-afflicted image I as a paradigmatic example, the atmospheric particulate matter simultaneously attenuates both the structural content and the chromatic style components of the image, precipitating a compound degradation.
The content features are corrupted because haze particles reduce the clarity of the structure of the objects. Style features are corrupted due to gray and blueish patterns introduced by haze.

The haze-induced degradation of content features manifests as a reduction in the structural legibility of depicted objects and their spatial arrangements, while the stylistic corruption is primarily characterized by the superimposition of achromatic and desaturated bluish-gray patterns attributable to the differential scattering of light wavelengths by the suspended aerosol particles.

Performing deep image enhancement without using paired samples of training data was proposed as an open problem. Here, paired-samples indicate the instances of the original image and corrupted image pairs.

The challenge of accomplishing deep image enhancement without recourse to paired training exemplars — that is, without access to corresponding clean-corrupted image dyads for supervisory guidance — was formally articulated as an unresolved open research problem, motivating the subsequent development of training-data-independent methodologies.
Recent advancement in deep internal learning solves the open problem for image restoration and image synthesis tasks.

The emergent paradigm of deep internal learning has demonstrated remarkable efficacy in resolving this longstanding open challenge, successfully accomplishing both image restoration and image synthesis objectives without requiring externally sourced paired training data, instead exploiting the intrinsic statistical regularities present within individual images.
We categorize deep internal learning methods for simplicity as: image reconstruction models, layer separation models, and single image GAN frameworks.

For the purposes of systematic exposition, deep internal learning methods are organized into three principal categories: image reconstruction models that regenerate clean imagery through iterative optimization, layer separation models that disentangle image components through joint decomposition, and single-image generative adversarial network frameworks that learn the internal patch distribution of a solitary image.

We formulate a generic framework called Deep Internal Learning for Image Enhancement. It does not use paired samples of training data and aims to learn features internally to perform image enhancement.

The proposed Deep Internal Learning for Image Enhancement framework, designated DILIE, constitutes a generalized computational paradigm that deliberately eschews reliance on externally paired training exemplars, instead harvesting representational knowledge from the internal statistical structure of the input image under consideration to accomplish the enhancement objective.
The good perceptual quality of DILIE framework is due to the ability of CNN to learn good quality image statistics from a single image.

The perceptual superiority of outputs generated by the DILIE framework can be fundamentally attributed to the remarkable capacity of convolutional neural networks to internalize high-fidelity image statistics from a solitary input image, thereby enabling effective feature learning in the conspicuous absence of large-scale annotated training corpora.

The DILIE framework performs content feature enhancement and style feature enhancement separately. Content feature enhancement decomposes the hazy image into environmental haze layer and haze-free image. Style feature enhancement transfers photo-realistic features from a style image.

The DILIE framework decomposes the overall enhancement task into two sequentially applied sub-modules that are designed and trained independently: the content feature enhancement component, which separates the hazy input into its constituent environmental haze layer and the latent haze-free image, followed by the style feature enhancement component, which instills photo-realistic or artistically stylized characteristics from a reference style image.

DILIE is a unified framework to restore the content features and synthesizes new style features for the image enhancement task. It takes the degraded image I as input and generates the enhanced image.

DILIE presents a holistic unified computational architecture that simultaneously attends to content feature restoration and style feature synthesis, receiving the degraded input image I and producing the perceptually enhanced output image through the sequential application of its constituent enhancement modules.

The encoder-decoder network f is used for the reconstruction or decomposition of input I. The style image S is used to enhance the style features of image I. The VGG19 network phi is used for image context learning and the style features enhancement.

An encoder-decoder network f serves as the primary computational workhorse for either reconstructing or decomposing the corrupted input, a supplementary style image S furnishes the stylistic reference signal guiding aesthetic enhancement, and the pre-trained VGG19 feature extractor phi provides the hierarchical representations necessary for context-preserving content loss computation and style feature matching.

Image decomposition improves the quality of images by separating image features and corrupted features. Formally, given an image I as a combination of image feature layer and environmental noise, decomposition separates I into the image features layer and the image corruption layer.

Image quality improvement through decomposition is achieved by algorithmically disentangling the clean image content from the superimposed corruption signal. Formally construed, the degraded observation I is modeled as an admixture of a latent clean feature layer and an environmental distortion layer, which the decomposition procedure seeks to isolate through simultaneous joint optimization of the respective network parameters.

The image decomposition in the basic form does not consider the context of the input image. The abstract information of content features represents the context of the image, i.e., objects and their relative positions.

A fundamental limitation of naive image decomposition formulations is their neglect of the semantic context embedded within the input image. This contextual information, encoded within the high-level content feature representations as an abstract description of the depicted objects and their relative spatial configurations, constitutes an essential constraint for producing semantically coherent decomposition results.

The contextual content loss is defined between the content features of the original image and the enhanced content image. LCL maximizes the contextual similarity between the enhanced image and the original to improve performance.

The contextual content loss LCL is formulated as a penalty term that promotes alignment between the high-level content feature representations extracted from the corrupted input and those of the content-enhanced output. By maximizing contextual feature similarity across these two representations, the loss function encourages the preservation of semantic coherence in the enhanced output, yielding measurably superior performance on dehazing benchmarks.
The content features are mostly present at the higher layers of feature extractor VGG19. The style features are mostly contained at the initial layers.

Within the hierarchical representational structure of VGG19, the content features encoding high-level semantic information are predominantly localized in the deeper layers of the network, while the style features capturing low-level chromatic and textural properties are primarily contained within the earlier shallow layers of the feature hierarchy.
Image reconstruction model uses encoder-decoder f to reconstruct the desired image. The output of CFE in image reconstruction is the network output for a given input.

The image reconstruction modality employs an encoder-decoder network f whose architectural inductive biases implicitly encode a powerful image prior, enabling the reconstruction of a clean image approximation from the corrupted input by iteratively minimizing a pixel-level discrepancy loss between the network output and a reference transformation of the input observation.
SFE aims to improve style features and output the enhanced image given the CFE output. SFE transfers the style features to the content-enhanced image using style image S.

Receiving the content-enhanced intermediate image produced by the content feature enhancement module as its input, the style feature enhancement component is tasked with transplanting stylistic characteristics harvested from the reference image S into this intermediate representation, thereby producing the final perceptually improved output image exhibiting the desired aesthetic qualities.

The style features enhancement is performed using the content loss and style loss. The content loss is defined between the content feature representations extracted from the content-enhanced image and the enhanced output.

Style feature enhancement is governed by a composite loss comprising two complementary terms: the content loss, which enforces consistency between the semantic content representations of the intermediate content-enhanced image and the final output, and the style loss, which penalizes discrepancies between the stylistic feature representations of the reference style image and those of the final output.

The photo-realism characterization in the image is an unsolved problem. The enhancement of the photo-realistic features is based on the observation that if the input image is photo-realistic, then those features could be retained with an affine loss.

Achieving faithful photo-realism in style-transferred outputs remains an unresolved challenge in computational imaging. The photo-realistic feature enhancement strategy herein rests on the theoretical insight that the photo-realistic character of an image can be preserved through the imposition of an affine color transformation constraint, effectively preventing the introduction of physically implausible cross-region color bleeding artifacts.

The total loss for photo-realistic enhancement includes an affine loss that preserves object structure while transforming the style features. The affine loss uses the Matting Laplacian of the input to transform the color distribution while preserving the object structure.

The composite loss function governing photo-realistic enhancement incorporates a Matting Laplacian-derived affine regularization term as its principal structural preservation mechanism. This affine constraint operates by restricting the color transformation to be locally affine within the image color space, thereby sanctioning stylistic chromatic modifications while simultaneously enforcing the geometric integrity of depicted objects and their boundaries.
The artistic feature enhancement allows small deformations to achieve an artistic look using relaxed earth mover distance to match the image feature distribution.

In contradistinction to photo-realistic enhancement, the artistic feature enhancement modality deliberately permits controlled geometric deformations in service of an aesthetically expressive outcome. Distribution matching between style and content features is accomplished through the relaxed earth mover distance, a geometrically-motivated optimal transport metric that accommodates pixel-level modifications while maintaining the overall structural composition.
Pictures taken in the hazy weather may lack scene information such as contrast, colors, and object structure. Haze is composed of small particles suspended in the gas.

Imagery acquired under adverse atmospheric conditions characterized by the presence of haze frequently exhibits pronounced deficiencies in contrast fidelity, chromatic saturation, and structural clarity, arising from the absorption and multiple-scattering effects of the suspended aerosol particles — minute solid or liquid particulates dispersed within the gaseous atmospheric medium.
The image degradation model for the hazy image is usually formulated using an atmospheric scattering model. The hazy image could be considered as a haze layer superimposed on the true scene content.

The physical mechanism underlying haze-induced image degradation is conventionally captured by the atmospheric scattering model, which decomposes the observed degraded image into two constituent elements: the attenuated true scene radiance scaled by a transmission map, and the additive airlight contribution, collectively conceptualized as a haze layer overlaid upon the latent haze-free scene.

Image dehazing can be formulated as a layer decomposition problem to separate the hazy image into a haze-free image layer and a haze layer, where the content-enhanced image is the approximation of the haze-free image.

Perhaps the most interesting result was the paradoxical impact that increased data volume and regularization had on classification performance. Although the highly-regularized dropout model learned more general features across both malware and goodware classes, its performance was substantially worse than a model with an older and smaller training set.

The most consequential and theoretically provocative finding concerns the inverse relationship between generalization quality and classification efficacy: despite acquiring more broadly applicable feature representations spanning both class populations, the aggressively regularized dropout model underperforms a model trained on an older, substantially smaller dataset — a paradox that complicates straightforward prescriptions for model improvement.

One explanation for this behavior is that malware-oriented features are strong indicators of class membership for both malware and goodware — similar to the way traditional antivirus signatures operate.

A plausible account for this counterintuitive dynamic is that features skewed toward the malware class function as strong bidirectional indicators — their presence signals malice while their absence signals benignity — echoing the asymmetric discriminative logic underlying signature-based antivirus detection.

Moreover, our results indicate that influential features are learned throughout the entire length of the input byte sequence, thereby providing evidence that the type of hierarchical architecture examined here may learn more diverse and robust features.

Beyond the qualitative similarity to expert-engineered features, the hierarchical pooling architecture distributes its most influential activations across the complete byte span of the input — a spatial breadth of coverage that suggests the model develops a more varied and resilient feature vocabulary than architectures limited to localized or header-region analysis.
